paragraphs.heading: Questions in my upper teens
paragraphs.edited: Since I grew up in a Christian home, the Christian story always made sense to me. My parents have worked their entire lives with a professional Christian ministry. My dad has spent his life writing, speaking and debating the truth of the Christian message. Yet when I was in my upper teens, I had some questions that kind of troubled me, that seemed more pertinent in my life than ever before. Questions like, how do I really know that Christianity is true? What if I was born in a different family or in a different culture, would I still believe the Christian message? What if my beliefs are false?

paragraphs.heading: Telling my dad
paragraphs.edited: I decided it was time to share my doubts and my questions with my father, not knowing how he would respond. After all, he spent his life teaching the Christian message to others. We were up in the mountains at a small coffee shop, and I remember leaning in to my dad and saying, Dad, I want to know what's true, but I don't know that I'm convinced that Christianity is true. And he instantly looked right back at me. He goes, son, I think that's great. And for a second I said, wait a minute, Dad, did you hear what I just said? I'm doubting Christianity. And he said, I did hear you, son, and I think this is good.

paragraphs.heading: Unexpressed doubts
paragraphs.edited: Doubts and questions are not bad. Whenever my students come up to me and say, hey, Mr. McDowell, I've got some questions and doubts, I always respond by saying, that's fantastic, I'm so glad you're asking these questions. Now, that's not the typical response that they expect, because sometimes we think that asking questions and doubting God and his Word can be bad. But that's not always the case. You see, doubts can be good if we see them as opportunities to go deeper in our faith. It's not doubts that are bad, it's unexpressed doubts that can be bad. You see, it's not doubts that are corrosive to faith. It's when we have doubts and we don't seek answers. So if you have doubts about your faith, the first thing to do is to just share them with somebody and start the conversation.

paragraphs.heading: Where a doubt really comes from
paragraphs.edited: There are a variety of reasons that might motivate someone to have questions and doubts. Some can certainly be intellectual, but I'm convinced that more often than not the source of a doubt, the heart of a doubt, comes from emotional, relational or moral reasons. Consider a couple of stories that might help.

paragraphs.edited: First, I met a young man while speaking at a conference in Chicago, and when I was done he came up to me and said, hey, can we go outside and talk a little further? I've got some questions for you, some doubts about my faith. I said, sure. So we went outside, and he had some questions about whether Jesus could really be God. He had questions about other religions. And after doing my best to answer his questions, I sensed that something deeper was going on. I said something to the effect of, you know, I'm answering your questions, but I think something else is going on with you. What is it?

paragraphs.heading: Relationships and how we see God
paragraphs.edited: Second, our relationships can deeply affect the way we relate to God. Take my father, for example. He had a distant and a drunk father, so he would hear people say things like, hey, you have a Heavenly Father who loves you, and my dad would think, wait a minute, father equals hurt and distance and pain. Why would I want a Heavenly Father when it just brings more pain? You see, the reality is our relationships, especially our broken relationships, can drive questions and doubts about God. An important question we really need to ask ourselves is, how have our relationships, the ones that have been good and the ones that have failed, affected the way we view and relate to God?

paragraphs.heading: John the Baptist's doubt
paragraphs.edited: Surprisingly, one of the most prominent examples of doubt in the Bible comes from John the Baptist, the prophesied forerunner of Christ the Messiah. Herod had John the Baptist arrested and thrown in prison, and he sends his disciples to Jesus to ask him, are you the one, or should we expect another? Well, the question is, why did John the Baptist have questions and doubts at this point in his life? And the answer is because he was alone and he was suffering. Loneliness and pain are common reasons why people have questions and doubts about God.

paragraphs.edited: Jesus's response is powerful. He doesn't scold John. He doesn't chastise him. He doesn't show disappointment in John for having questions and doubts. Rather, he gives John evidence. In Luke 7:22 through 23, it describes how Jesus says to his disciples, go back and tell John what you have seen and what you have heard. The deaf hear, the blind see, the lame walk, and the dead live again, and the poor have the good news preached to them.

paragraphs.edited: So what does this tell us? Well, for one thing, it tells us that doubts are a normal and natural part of life. All of us should expect to have questions at some point in our journey of faith. In fact, even the apostles had doubts. It says in Matthew 28 that they worshiped Jesus as God, and yet some of them doubted. Can you imagine that? The very people who saw the risen Jesus had doubts. If John the Baptist and the apostles had doubts, you better believe that some of us, if not most of us, will have doubts at some point in our life. That's why I believe that Jude 22 says to have mercy on those who doubt.

paragraphs.heading: Doubt is not the opposite of faith
paragraphs.edited: Doubt is not the opposite of faith. In fact, doubt can often serve as the basis for developing a more robust faith. The key is to identify what is the source of the doubt. If your doubts are emotional, you might need to find and experience some emotional healing. If your doubts are relational, you might need to restore some broken relationships. And if your doubts are intellectual, you need to find some answers to your questions. You see, doubt is not necessarily corrosive to faith, but can be the opportunity to develop a deeper and a lasting faith.
